rtk filters and compresses command output before it hits your LLM context. One Rust binary, 100+ commands, under 10ms overhead.

It optimizes tokens for any agent: compressing, routing, and filtering what your AI reads and sends. The pipeline is composable, and it's built on RTK's bash-output compression, which cuts output by up to 90%.

Angular builds work through rtk ng build: compact build tables, every bundle and diagnostic kept.

Browser Use is an open-source browser agent. Run it locally with any LLM, or on Browser Use Cloud, where stealth browsers start at $0.02/hour and the agent scores 90.5% on Stealth Bench V2.

It browses like you do. Give it a task and it will find an available slot, pick a date and time, handle the CAPTCHA, and book your driving test.

Three ways to run it. Need to scale? Take Path 1, the Fully Hosted Cloud: hosted agent, hosted browser. Just automating your own browsing? Path 2 is the CLI. Building your own thing? Path 3, the Python Library, runs the open source agent locally from your code.

Paperclip is the app people use to manage AI agents for work.

It's open-source orchestration for teams of AI agents. If OpenClaw is an employee, Paperclip is the company that employs it.

Paperclip is a Node.js server and React UI that orchestrates a team of AI agents to run a business. You bring your own agents, assign goals, and track work and costs from one dashboard. Pick models and harnesses per agent. Your team's tasks, skills, permissions, and history stay in one place.

It looks like a task manager. Under the hood: org charts, budgets, governance, goal alignment, agent coordination. You manage business goals, not pull requests.

Any agent that can receive a heartbeat counts as hired. Custom processes, HTTP endpoints, and external adapter packages extend the roster. See the adapter overview for setup and capabilities.

Agentic Awesome Skills — AI Skills & AAS Core

AAS Core lets Codex or Claude search the complete local catalog, record which skills the agent picks, and preview a plan before anything touches your target. Core does not rank or recommend skills.

Cut agent token spend by 80%. Graphify Cloud is always-on memory that governs your agents, keeps code quality high, and proves correctness with formal verification. Start a free 14-day trial.

Type /graphify in your AI coding assistant. It maps your entire project (code, docs, PDFs, images, videos) into a knowledge graph you can query instead of grepping through files.

Code maps are free and fully local. Code is parsed with tree-sitter AST: deterministic, no LLM, nothing leaves your machine. Docs, PDFs, images and video use your assistant's model, or a configured API key, for a semantic pass.

Every edge is explained. Each connection is tagged EXTRACTED (explicit in the source) or INFERRED (resolved by graphify), so you know what was read directly and what was inferred.

This is not a vector index. No embeddings, no vector store. It's a real graph you traverse: ask a question, trace the path between two things, or explain one concept.

Want it always-on? Graphify Cloud keeps the graph live across your entire SDLC: monorepo and cross-repo support, formal verification, and code review with a bird's-eye view of your SDLC, plus connectors for Sentry, Jira, and more so incidents and tickets sit in the same graph as your code. Start a free 14-day trial at app.graphify.com.

Codewhale is an open-source coding agent that lives in your terminal and works with any model. Hand it a task and it reads your repository, edits files, and runs commands until the job is done or it needs something from you. It ships with more than 40 built-in providers, defaults to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and runs models on your own machine too. Type /receipts to see every file it changed, command it ran, and web or MCP call it made.

The demo is a 0.10.2 development build with a scripted test model, run in Full Access inside a throwaway workspace. The edit, three tests and a sub-agent review all ran for real.

Check out the Codewhale × OrcaRouter offer. Codewhale earns a referral fee from OrcaRouter.

Use Repomix online at repomix.com. Got questions? Join us on Discord. Share your experience and tips, hear about new features first, and get help with configuration and usage.

Repomix packs your entire repository into one AI-friendly file. Use it whenever you need to feed your codebase to Large Language Models (LLMs) or tools like Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Gemini, Gemma, Llama, Grok, and more.

If Repomix saves you time, please consider sponsoring me.

codebase-memory-mcp is an MCP server that gives your coding agent local code intelligence. It builds a persistent knowledge graph on your machine, connecting source code, documentation, configuration, and infrastructure. When you need to find an unfamiliar feature, follow a call across services, trace a deployment back to its source, or check what a change could break, you query the graph.

The MCP server is the core. Your agent gets structural context through the Model Context Protocol, or you can query the graph yourself from the CLI. There's also an optional visual companion, CBM Lens, in open beta (v0.0.1): a source reader, architecture maps, the Galaxy graph, coverage diagnostics, architecture decisions, and local code chat.

Under the hood, a native C backend exposes 17 MCP tools, parses languages and file formats with vendored grammars, and adds Hybrid LSP type resolution for supported languages. The installer handles 45 automatic or conditional client integrations, including client configuration, skills, agent profiles, and applicable hooks. Indexing and graph queries run locally. No hosted service, no API key. Focused graph queries can cut repeated file reads and token use; see the measured results.

Archon builds the software that builds your software.

Write a workflow in YAML, and Archon runs it with AI agents, scripts, and your own decisions where they're needed. The first factory it ships with is software: the bundled SDLC pack takes an issue through to a merged pull request. The same engine runs any process you can describe.

You stay on top of the process instead of inside it. Runs do the work, queues keep it moving, and a run only reaches you when it needs a decision you own.

OpenCLI turns any website into a CLI and runs Browser Use on your logged-in Chrome. Websites and browser sessions become deterministic interfaces for humans and AI agents. Or point Browser Use at any page: move through it, fill forms, click, extract, automate.

It's a general-purpose browser automation CLI for AI agents, and an agent-browser alternative. You can inspect, click, fill forms, extract, and screenshot websites without a site adapter. Built-in adapters add reusable, deterministic site commands. See OpenCLI vs agent-browser and migration.

One surface, three ways to automate:

- Built-in adapters for sites like Bilibili, Zhihu, Xiaohongshu, Reddit, HackerNews, Twitter/X, and many more.
- Your AI agent can operate any website. Install the opencli-browser skill in Claude Code, Cursor, or similar, and it clicks, types, fills, extracts, and inspects any page through your logged-in browser via opencli browser primitives.
- Write new adapters end-to-end with opencli browser plus the opencli-adapter-author skill. It walks you from first recon through field decoding, code, and opencli adapter test.

Moli is a production-ready headless browser built for AI agents. It loads and renders pages on demand, so you get a full browser runtime without the heavy footprint.

Point your agent at it to fetch and extract pages, search the web, or automate browser tasks. Drive it from the CLI, CDP, WebDriver Classic, or WebDriver BiDi. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

Pick your models and use them with Codex, Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Grok Build. Connect OpenCode, Pi, Qoder, WorkBuddy, Kilo, Cline, T3 Code and more through managed configs. See every supported tool on the client support page.

opencodex is a lightweight local gateway between your coding tools and your model providers. It accepts the Responses, Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages APIs, then translates each request into whatever your provider speaks. Streaming, tool calls, reasoning and images pass through wherever the client, model and provider support them. So you can run Claude, Gemini, Grok, GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, Ollama and other providers with Codex, Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Grok Build.

It also manages a ChatGPT account pool for Codex auth. Add accounts and refresh their quotas in the dashboard. New sessions route to the lowest-usage healthy account; existing threads stay pinned to the account that started them.

A Claude skill that writes accurate prompts for any AI tool. You stop wasting tokens and credits on re-prompting, and you get the answer you should have gotten on attempt one. It holds full context and keeps memory across the session.

It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Grok, Gemini, o1/o3, MiniMax, Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Bolt, v0, Lovable, Devin, Perplexity, Midjourney, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, ComfyUI, Sora, Runway, ElevenLabs, Zapier, Make, and any other AI tool you point it at.

Nanobrowser is an open-source AI agent that runs in your own browser. Type a task into the side panel and it reads pages, clicks, types and switches tabs until the job is done. It won't submit, send, delete or upload anything without asking you first.

Download it free from the Chrome Web Store. Talk to other users on Discord and X, or sponsor the project. Donations keep Nanobrowser free and open source.

Rowboat is an open-source AI assistant with docs, a whiteboard, and email built in. Use it alone or with your team.

It indexes your work into a living knowledge graph, then uses that graph to get work done on your machine. You get surfaces for working with AI: an email client, notes, a browser, code mode, a meeting note taker, and workspaces for each project.

Those are the skills installed directly. Want it all in one command? ARIS also ships as a standalone CLI and as plugins.

The ARIS family runs the same method on other jobs, one line each. Details live in their own repos.

EasyAIOffer: 34 bilingual ML and LLM interview cheat sheets on one page, with derivations, from-scratch PyTorch, and 25 questions each. Built so autumn recruiting goes a little easier.

LifeOS is a general purpose AI harness, built for doing anything you want to do in life and work with AI. It captures who you are, what you care about, and where you're trying to go, then uses AI that knows you to help you get there.

Because it has your full context, it makes what you do more efficient and effective, whether that's building apps, starting a business, or working on creative projects.

The whole system works on one central concept: moving from your Current State to your Ideal State, in pursuit of Euphoric Surprise.

Instatic

A self-hosted CMS where the visual editor, content engine, and publisher all run in one Bun server. The pages it ships are clean enough to read in view-source.

Watch the introductory video about Instatic on YouTube.

Building a modern website usually means stacking pieces: a headless CMS, a framework, a host, a form service, an analytics vendor, an image CDN. Each has its own bill, its own dashboard, its own 2 a.m. outage. Instatic runs the whole thing in one Bun server instead: the canvas editor, the content engine, media, auth, forms, plugins, and the publisher. You host it wherever you like, on SQLite or Postgres.

Then there's what it hands back. Most builders quietly give up on clean output. Instatic doesn't. You get plain semantic HTML and compact CSS, with none of the editor's machinery left in the page. No framework runtime, no builder attributes, no div soup. The site loads like a static file because, most of the time, it is one.

The Replica skill

Eleven Claude skills that clone any app. Free, MIT. No signup, no API key, nothing to connect.

One reverse-engineers the app you want to clone. One rebuilds it. One hunts for bugs. And one is the Entrepreneur: it reads what that app's users hate and fixes it in yours, so you end up with something you can sell.

Mission Control

A self-hosted control plane for running AI agents.

Dispatch tasks, inspect runs, review failures, track spend, coordinate agent runtimes. All from one local dashboard, backed by SQLite.

It's open source, built by Builderz Labs and maintained by nyk. Works with OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, and other runtimes. It isn't part of any one of them.

One warning: this is alpha software. APIs, schemas, and configuration may change between releases. Read the security guidance before exposing it to a network.

Autoresearch turns Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse into an engine that keeps improving your code while you sleep. It's built on Karpathy's autoresearch: set a constraint, attach a mechanical metric, let the agent iterate on its own. The gains compound.

Here's the whole deal. You set the GOAL. The agent runs the LOOP. You wake up to results. You don't need AGI for this. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that doesn't quit.

All five tools are supported for the core skill, the bundled runtime, installation, and verification. Hook guardrails ship for Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

When your metric loop stalls, fork-and-flush breaks the plateau, the way Cai et al. did (arXiv:2610.07447). At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with nothing kept, the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches pick their own ideas; the other half each get a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). Running Guided, R sets the split. The orchestrator hits a plateau and answers with FORK before it gives up. Full details in guide/autoresearch.md.

You get an interface around the pi coding agent, workspaces that isolate each change, and durable project knowledge stored as living specs and reusable skills. Next we're adding full extension support, so ThinkRail will create the tools it needs based on how you actually work.

Agent skills are simple text files that teach AI assistants (like Claude, Copilot, or Codex) how to do new things on demand, without retraining. This is a community-maintained list of them. Unlike bulk-generated skill repositories, the collection focuses on real-world Agent Skills created and used by actual engineering teams. The skills are compatible with Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, and more.

OUROBOROS

The agent gets smarter on its own. We just hold the line.

Skip prompt engineering. The agent runs, fails, and gets smarter every generation. The grading command and expected result never enter the success contract we hand it.

Ouroboros is an Agent OS for replayable AI coding workflows.

One command installs it. Then run it once inside your coding agent. Details in the Quick Start. There are demo videos for each runtime.

Give it a vague idea and it returns a verified, working codebase, across Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Hermes, Gemini, Kiro, Copilot, Pi, OMP, Zcode, Goose, GJC, Antigravity, and Grok.

Ouroboros is an Agent OS for AI coding: a local-first runtime layer that turns non-deterministic agent work into a replayable, observable, policy-bound execution contract. Instead of ad-hoc prompting, you get a structured specification-first workflow: interview, crystallize, execute, evaluate, evolve.

Development guide

Monid (OpenRouter for agent tools)

OpenRouter, but for agent tools. Your agent gets one base URL and one key, and through them reaches 2,000+ tools across 72+ providers: web search and scraping, people and company enrichment, social platforms, reviews and market data, and video, image and voice generation.

If you're an AI agent, fetch `` and save it to your skill directory. It handles the rest.

This repo is the connector layer: one generic framework describing every endpoint above. It covers how each is called, what it accepts, what it returns, and how its usage is counted. Connectors are declarative, so a coding agent can write one. Point it at your API docs and this repo, and adding your API to Monid becomes a pull request.

Code-Graph-RAG parses your multi-language codebase with Tree-sitter, and sharpens that parse with compiler-grade frontends and runtime traces where they exist. It turns the structure into a knowledge graph stored in an embedded graph database, so there's no server to run. Then you ask it questions, edit code, and optimise, all in plain English. A monorepo of mixed languages? One unified graph schema covers it.

1. Index: it parses your repository into a knowledge graph, fast.
2. Ask: it answers your questions and edits your code, grounded in that graph.

fallow is codebase intelligence for TypeScript and JavaScript. Point it at your repository and it maps health, complexity, duplication, architecture, styling, and unused code from one graph.

You get a single Rust binary. It doesn't need the TypeScript compiler, and you don't configure anything to start.

Run it in the root of any JS or TS project. On a fictional storefront monorepo, a pull request gate might look like this:

Illustrative output for a fictional project. The gate fails with exit code 1 when it finds issues in changed files. Issues that existed before the change are excluded.

Under the hood, fallow builds a graph of your modules, exports, dependencies, functions, and styling tokens. Its analyses read that graph to report complexity, architecture drift, duplication, unused code, and risks in a pull request.

You can run fallow in four places. All four read the same config file and use the same analysis engine.

Bumblebee collects package, extension, and developer-tool metadata from macOS and Linux developer endpoints. It's read-only.

It answers one narrow supply-chain question: an advisory names a package, extension, or version. Which of your developer machines have a match in their on-disk metadata right now?

SBOMs tell you what shipped. EDR tells you what ran or touched the network. Response work often needs a third view: the messy local state sitting in lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, and supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee reads that scattered state and turns it into structured NDJSON component records. Hand it an exposure catalog and it flags exact matches. You already know what you're looking for; this gives you a fast, read-only check.

CLI Printing Press

For an AI agent, time and money come down to two things: speed and token spend. A well-designed CLI becomes muscle memory for the agent. No hunting through docs, no wrong turns, no wasted tokens. So we built the Printing Press to print the best CLIs in the world for agents.

It reads the official API docs, studies every popular community CLI and MCP server, and sniffs the web for the APIs nobody published (think Google Flights or Dominos). Then it applies the power-user playbook Peter Steinberger proved with discrawl and gogcli: local SQLite, compound commands, agent-native flags. Out comes a token-efficient Go CLI, a Claude Code skill, and an MCP server, for any API or any website.

Three CLIs printed by the press, installable today:

ACI: Open-Source Infra to Power Unified MCP Servers and VibeOps

This repo is for the ACI.dev platform. Want the Unified MCP server built with ACI.dev? See aci-mcp.

ACI.dev is an open-source tool-calling platform that connects 600+ tools to any agentic IDE or custom AI agent. Agents get intent-aware access to tools, with multi-tenant auth, granular permissions, and dynamic tool discovery, exposed as direct function calls or through a Unified Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server.

Say you're building against Google Calendar, Slack, and a dozen other services. Instead of writing separate OAuth flows and API clients for each, ACI.dev manages the authentication and hands your agents unified, secure function calls. Reach those capabilities through the Unified MCP server or the lightweight Python SDK, which works with any LLM framework.

Add one unified MCP server to your favourite agentic IDE and you can vibe code and automate devOps in the same session. Configure the MCP with Vercel, Supabase, Cloudflare, and other platforms, then let AI handle provisioning, deployment, database configs, and debugging. That's how a vibe coded prototype becomes a live product.

SkillsBench tests whether AI agents can actually use Skills to finish professional work across different domains. It measures how much better a model gets at solving complex real-world tasks when specialized Skills are available.

We adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting to test something the original setup can't: what happens when many Skills are installed at once. Normally, each task comes with just its own specialized Skill. In our version, every task runs in a global environment with all 195 specialized Skills installed, and nothing else changes. The question is whether an agent can find the right Skills in that large pool, pick them out, and organize them into a workflow that gets the task done.

We ran vibeskills v4.1.0 through SkillsBench using DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline setup. Against the baseline without vibeskills, the mean verifier reward went up 21.12 percentage points. Token consumption dropped 29.6%. Tool calls dropped 33.1%.

Agentic Context Engine (ACE)

ACE is the open-source engine behind Kayba. If you'd rather have the whole loop managed for you, from investigating failures to shipping fixes as PRs, get a demo.

Your AI agent repeats the same mistakes every session. It forgets what worked and ignores what failed. ACE, an open-source engine, adds a persistent learning loop: it records what the agent got wrong, reflects on the error, and feeds that back so the next attempt goes better without you touching anything. Watch it work: an agent claims a seahorse emoji exists, ACE reflects on the error, and the next attempt comes back correct.

Don't want to run it yourself? Kayba is the managed service that runs this loop for your production agents automatically.
